item.description:
Authors: Regina M. Simeone, Laura D. Zambrano, Margaret M. Newhams, Amanda B. Payne, Amber O. Orzel-Lockwood, Natasha B. Halasa, Jemima Calixte, Aline B. Maddux, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641333
Abstract: Importance Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospitalization rates are highest among children younger than 2 years. For certain high-risk children entering their second RSV season, the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab is recommended. Little is known regarding preexisting health conditions as risk factors for RSV-related respiratory failure in children during their second RSV season. Objective To describe children admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for severe RSV by classifying them by their nirsevimab eligibility status and preexisting health conditions, and comparing their demographic and clinical characteristics. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study analyzed US children aged 8 to 23 months admitted to the PICU in 30 pediatric hospitals in the 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025 RSV seasons. All children had an RSV-positive result from a respiratory sample and received respiratory support with high-flow nasal cannula, noninvasive ventilation, or invasive mechanical ventilation. Analyses were based on the US criteria for second-season nirsevimab eligibility as recommended in August 2023. Exposure Preexisting health conditions potentially associated with increased risk of severe RSV disease. Patients were classified into 4 mutually exclusive groups of eligibility status and preexisting health conditions: (1) met nirsevimab eligibility criteria, (2) with other identified RSV risk conditions (with some evidence of increased risk for severe RSV), (3) with other preexisting conditions, and (4) with no preexisting conditions. Main Outcomes and Measures Patient demographic characteristics and level of respiratory support received were compared by level of preexisting health conditions. Results A total of 574 children (median [IQR] age, 1.2 [1.1-1.5] years; 317 males [55.2%]) were included. Overall, 47 patients (8.2%) met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria, 76 (13.2%) had other identified RSV risk conditions, 96 (16.7%) had other preexisting conditions, and 355 (61.8%) had no preexisting conditions. A higher proportion of children who met nirsevimab eligibility criteria required invasive mechanical ventilation vs children with other identified RSV risk conditions, those with other preexisting health conditions, or those with no preexisting health conditions (40.4% [19 of 47] vs 17.1% [13 of 76], 10.4% [10 of 96], 5.9% [21 of 355]; P for trend &amp;lt;.001). Conclusions and Relevance Among children admitted to the PICU for severe RSV, 8.2% met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria and 13.2% had other identified RSV risk conditions. These findings might help inform future deliberations regarding second RSV season recommendations for nirsevimab eligibility in the US.

Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644986
Abstract: Importance Not all men with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) receive the recommended combination therapy of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) plus an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) and/or chemotherapy. Objective To determine factors associated with combination therapy use among veterans with mCSPC in the national Veterans Health Administration (VHA) system. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study included US veterans diagnosed with mCSPC between January 1, 2023, through December 31, 2024, who were followed up through June 30, 2025. National multicenter data were obtained from the VHA electronic health record, community care settings (private care paid with VHA benefits), and Medicare. All included veterans were identified through a validated natural language processing algorithm, were followed up in the VHA for at least 2 years prior to their metastatic diagnosis, were provided ADT within the first 6 months of diagnosis, and received no prostate cancer–directed therapy in the year prior to diagnosis. Exposure Clinical factors (eg, comorbidities, frailty, prostate cancer burden at diagnosis) and nonclinical factors (eg, annual household income, neighborhood disadvantage) were investigated to determine their association with the outcome. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was receipt of combination therapy (ie, ADT plus ARPI [abiraterone, enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide] and/or docetaxel) vs ADT alone. Information on these treatments was obtained through pharmacy records. Multilevel logistic regression models were used and marginal predicted probabilities were reported to determine the associations of factors with receipt of combination therapy. Variation among VHA facilities was reported. Results A total of 4023 veterans (mean [SD] age, 75.3 [8.0] years) met eligibility criteria. Of these patients, 2339 (58.1%) had de novo metastatic disease, while 1684 (41.9%) had recurrent disease. Overall, 2564 patients (63.7%) received combination therapy. In adjusted analyses, older veterans (eg, aged 85-89 years: predicted probability, −14.1 [95% CI, −20.5 to −8.2] percentage points [pp]) and veterans with more comorbidities (eg, congestive heart failure: predicted probability, −7.5 [95% CI, −12.9 to −2.5] pp) were less likely to receive combination therapy. Annual household income and neighborhood disadvantage were not associated with receipt of combination therapy. Patients treated by urologists were less likely to receive combination therapy than patients treated by hematologist-oncologists (predicted probability, −23.7 [95% CI, −27.4 to −19.6] pp). Use of combination therapy ranged from 34% to 78% among VHA facilities. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of veterans with de novo and recurrent mCSPC, receipt of combination therapy was high; annual household income and neighborhood disadvantage had no association with treatment use. The study findings suggest that the region where a veteran lives, the facility where they receive care, and the type of cancer specialist they see are factors of the variation in combination therapy use that need further exploration.

Abstract: Importance Compression-only cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CO-CPR) has been widely promoted to encourage bystander intervention in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but long-term trends in bystander CPR and the associations between CPR type and outcomes in pediatric OHCA remain unclear. Objective To evaluate temporal trends in bystander CPR type and the associations with clinical outcomes among children with OHCA in Japan. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study included patients aged 17 years or younger with known receipt of bystander CPR documented in the nationwide All-Japan Utstein Registry from January 1, 2005, to December 31, 2023. Data analysis was performed from November 24, 2025, to September 2, 2026, including additional analyses conducted during the revision process. Exposures Bystander CPR was categorized as rescue-breathing CPR (RB-CPR), CO-CPR, or no bystander CPR. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate; secondary outcomes were 30-day survival rate and prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Temporal trends were assessed with multinomial logistic regression, and associations between CPR type and outcomes were evaluated using modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation, with CO-CPR serving as the reference. Results Among 26 785 pediatric patients with OHCA (median [IQR] age, 2.0 [0-12] years; 16 254 males [60.7%]), 6543 (24.4%) received RB-CPR, 9112 (34.0%) received CO-CPR, and 11 130 (41.6%) received no bystander CPR. The adjusted probability of CO-CPR increased from 14.6% (95% CI, 13.1%-16.1%) in 2005 to 55.1% (95% CI, 52.5%-57.6%) in 2023, whereas RB-CPR declined from 41.7% (95% CI, 39.7%-43.7%) to 10.4% (95% CI, 8.7%-12.1%). The adjusted probability of receiving no bystander CPR plateaued at approximately 35.0% after 2013. Neurologically favorable 30-day survival rate occurred in 3.6% receiving no bystander CPR, 9.5% receiving CO-CPR, and 16.0% receiving RB-CPR. Compared with CO-CPR, RB-CPR was associated with a higher 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 1.71; 95% CI, 1.57-1.86), 30-day survival rate (ARR, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.42-1.61), and prehospital ROSC (ARR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.51-1.75), whereas receipt of no bystander CPR was associated with lower probabilities of these outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of children with OHCA, increasing CO-CPR use coincided with declining RB-CPR but not with further reductions in untreated arrests after 2013. No bystander CPR was associated with worse outcomes compared with CO-CPR and RB-CPR. RB-CPR had more favorable outcomes than CO-CPR, supporting the continued importance of rescue breathing in pediatric resuscitation.

item.title: Commercial Health Care Prices and Medical Debt in the US
item.dc:creator: Fredric Blavin
Breno Braga
Avani Pugazhendhi
Renee Wu
item.description:
Authors: Fredric Blavin, Breno Braga, Avani Pugazhendhi, Renee Wu
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643409
Abstract: Importance Medical debt remains a major source of financial strain for US households. Although commercial health care prices vary substantially across markets, little is known about how these prices are associated with medical debt. Objective To examine the association between changes in commercial to Medicare price ratios and changes in medical debt in collections across US local markets. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study used data from multiple geographic areas (referred to hereinafter as geozips ) in the US. Commercial to Medicare price ratio data were obtained from FAIR Health claims for 2020 and 2022 to 2023, and medical debt outcomes were measured using the Urban Institute Credit Panel in August 2020 and August 2023. Analyses were conducted between October 2025 and August 2026 at the geozip level using a 2-period ecologic first-difference model. Exposures Changes in commercial to Medicare price ratios for professional, outpatient, and inpatient services. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the change in the share of adults with with medical debt in collections exceeding $500. Results The sample included 479 geozips in the US. A 1-unit increase in the professional commercial to Medicare price ratio was associated with a 4.3–percentage point increase (0.043; 95% CI, 0.027-0.060; P &amp;lt; .001) in the share of adults with medical debt in collections above $500. Changes in the inpatient and outpatient price ratios were not statistically associated with medical debt in collections exceeding $500. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of US geozips from 2020 to 2023, increases in commercial to Medicare price ratios for professional services were associated with increases in medical debt in collections, whereas changes in inpatient and outpatient price ratios were not. These findings suggest that commercial price increases in services more directly tied to patient cost sharing coincide with increased financial hardship.

item.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Alcohol Use Disorder Treatment for Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease
item.dc:creator: Annabel Gerber
Alice Agyekum
Jeong Yun Yang
Sheril Varghese
Cadence Chang
Avesh J. Thuluvath
Elizabeth C. Verna
Gene Y. Im
item.description:
Authors: Annabel Gerber, Alice Agyekum, Jeong Yun Yang, Sheril Varghese, Cadence Chang, Avesh J. Thuluvath, Elizabeth C. Verna, Gene Y. Im, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644980
Abstract: Importance Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) is a leading cause of liver-related mortality and liver transplant. Combined behavioral interventions (CBI) and medications for alcohol use disorder (MAUD) are underutilized. Thus, it is critical to identify optimal therapeutic and cost-effective windows for CBI and MAUD in patients with ALD at earlier fibrosis stages. Objective To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of naltrexone and CBI in preventing cirrhosis in patients with ALD compared with no treatment. Design, Setting, and Participants This economic evaluation used a Markov state-transition model simulating lifetime disease progression and health care costs associated with ALD. The simulated patient cohort began at 45 years of age with active AUD and stage 3 fibrosis (F3) and could experience progression to compensated or decompensated cirrhosis. Exposure All patients were assumed to complete a 16-week course of naltrexone along with 52 weeks of CBI. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes included total health care cost, quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios. Secondary outcomes included liver-related mortality and progression to compensated and decompensated cirrhosis. Scenario and sensitivity analyses were performed to determine outcomes at earlier stages and with varied cost and model parameters. Results Without intervention, 61% of the cohort died from liver-related causes, 88% developed compensated cirrhosis, and 66% of those experienced progression to decompensated cirrhosis, with a lifetime cost of $79 799 per person. With treatment initiated at F3, liver-related mortality was reduced to 58%, lifetime compensated cirrhosis to 87%, and lifetime progression to decompensated cirrhosis to 62%, with a lifetime cost of $78 673. The treatment strategy dominated because the lifetime costs were lower and more QALYs were gained when compared with untreated natural history. Treatment was preferred in sensitivity analyses at relapse rates to 100% and adherence greater than 0%, in scenario analyses when treatment was initiated at stages F2 and F1, and for the models including societal and AUD costs. Conclusions and Relevance In this economic evaluation of AUD treatment for patients with ALD, treating patients with ALD with naltrexone and CBI at F3 saved cost and was more effective than no treatment, reducing progression to compensated and decompensated cirrhosis. The results remained true at stages F1 and F2 fibrosis and when considering the societal costs and the costs of AUD. Future studies should include prospective evaluations of screening strategies combined with early treatment, as many patients are diagnosed at advanced stages of ALD.

item.title: Sleep-Wake Cycle Profiles and Incident Dementia and Cognitive Decline in Older Adults
item.dc:creator: Sam Vidil
Ian Meneghel Danilevicz
Aline Dugravot
Clémence Cavaillès
Nathalia Garcia Ocampo
Archana Singh-Manoux
Séverine Sabia
item.description:
Authors: Sam Vidil, Ian Meneghel Danilevicz, Aline Dugravot, Clémence Cavaillès, Nathalia Garcia Ocampo, Archana Singh-Manoux, Séverine Sabia
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644843
Abstract: Importance Sleep-wake cycle (SWC) disruptions are common in patients with dementia and potentially also in the preclinical phase of the disease. Accelerometers allow objective measures of multiple SWC dimensions: rest-activity rhythm (RAR), daytime activity, sleep, and chronotype, but these dimensions are rarely examined together. Objective This study examined the association of SWC profiles, incorporating the 4 SWC dimensions, with incident dementia and cognitive decline. Design, Setting, and Participants Prospective, UK population-based cohort study based on accelerometer data from the 2012 to 2013 wave of the Whitehall II cohort study, with a median (IQR) follow-up of 12.3 (12.0-12.7) years. Statistical analyses were conducted from June 2025 to March 2026. Participants were dementia-free aged 60 years or older with valid accelerometer data and covariates at baseline. Exposure Nine SWC profiles derived from 36 SWC metrics. Main Outcomes and Measures Incident dementia cases until March 2025 were retrieved from electronic health records. Cognitive tests were administered in 2012 to 2013, 2015 to 2016, and 2019 to 2022 and each test score was standardized based on 2012 to 2013 data and all tests averaged to derive a global cognitive z score. Results Among 3973 participants (median [IQR] age = 68.4 [64.7 to 74.0] years; 26% women), 379 dementia cases were recorded during a median 12.3-year follow-up. Compared with participants with robust RAR (high level and amplitude, stable, not fragmented), light-intensity physical activity (PA) and good sleep (profile 3), those with poorer RAR (low level and amplitude, unstable, fragmented) along with low PA and poor sleep (profile 7), or with high level and low amplitude RAR and restless sleep (profile 8) had higher dementia risk (hazard ratio, 1.94 [95% CI, 1.32 to 2.84], and 1.96 [95% CI, 1.27 to 3.03], respectively). In analyses on cognitive decline (3806 participants), profile 7 as well as the most sedentary profile with the poorest RAR (profile 9) had faster 10-year cognitive decline (−0.14 [95% CI, −0.26 to −0.02]) and −0.28 [95% CI, −0.44 to −0.13], respectively). Cognitive outcomes in participants with robust RAR and higher PA were similar, irrespective of sleep. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 3973 older adults, consideration of all SWC dimensions was important in identifying profiles associated with cognitive outcomes; further studies are needed to evaluate whether SWC interventions reduce the risk or delay onset of dementia.

item.title: Prevalence of Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Without Contact Sport Repetitive Head Impact Exposure
item.dc:creator: Michael J. Mastrodicasa
Grace H. Olson
Raymond C. Guo
Charlotte B. Luster
Nick C. Hernandez
Evan D. Feigel
Irving Zhao
Nathan E. Howarth
item.description:
Authors: Michael J. Mastrodicasa, Grace H. Olson, Raymond C. Guo, Charlotte B. Luster, Nick C. Hernandez, Evan D. Feigel, Irving Zhao, Nathan E. Howarth, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643928
Abstract: Importance A pooled baseline prevalence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in populations without repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure is needed to contextualize prevalence in other cohorts. Objective To estimate the pooled prevalence of CTE in populations without documented contact sport–based RHI exposure. Data Sources PubMed and Embase were searched from inception through February 23, 2026, using terms for CTE, prevalence, epidemiology, and neuropathology. Study Selection Studies reporting CTE prevalence in cohorts without documented contact sport RHI history were included and classified by ascertainment rigor into a primary group with verified absence of contact sport RHI or a secondary unscreened reference cohort. Studies were excluded for cohort overlap or for RHI-linked comorbid conditions (eg, epilepsy). Data Extraction and Synthesis Data were independently extracted by 2 authors, with discrepancy resolved by a third. Risk of bias and quality were assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Heterogeneity ( I 2 and τ 2 ) and robustness (leave-one-out sensitivity analysis) were assessed. Main Outcomes and Measures Confirmed CTE in individuals without documented contact sport RHI history was estimated using pooled prevalence and 95% CIs. Results Twelve cohort studies (4421 individuals; weighted mean age at death, 75.1 years; 2481 male [56.1%]) were identified. In the primary analysis of 7 cohorts with verified absence of contact sport RHI (1604 individuals), 12 cases of CTE were identified (crude prevalence, 0.75% [95% CI, 0.43%-1.30%]); pooled prevalence was 1.06% (95% CI, 0.10%-10.79%), reflecting substantial heterogeneity ( I 2 = 87.0%) and limited precision from few cases and presence of an outlier with 5 of 7 individuals with CTE. Excluding the outlier yielded a pooled prevalence of 0.70% (95% CI, 0.28%-1.74%) and reduced heterogeneity ( I 2 = 6.6%). In the 5 unscreened reference cohorts (2817 individuals), 17 cases of CTE were identified (crude prevalence, 0.60% [95% CI, 0.38%-0.96%]). Across all 12 cohorts, the crude prevalence was 0.66% (95% CI, 0.46%-0.94%), and the pooled prevalence was 0.85% (95% CI, 0.24%-2.89%). Conclusions and Relevance This systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 cohort studies not selected for contact sport–based RHI exposure found that CTE pathology was rare, with a baseline prevalence of approximately 1%. These findings provide a reference point for interpreting CTE prevalence in other populations, including cohorts with contact sport exposure.

item.title: Firearm Homicide Surges From 1979 to 2023
item.dc:creator: Andrew R. Morral
Rosanna Smart
item.description:
Authors: Andrew R. Morral, Rosanna Smart
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644022
Abstract: Importance US firearm homicide rates surged twice in the past 35 years. Better understanding of such surges could aid prevention. Objective To compare the demographic and geographic distribution of surge deaths and examine state-level correlates of surge severity across the 1985-1993 and 2014-2021 firearm homicide surge periods. Design, Setting, and Participants This serial cross-sectional study obtained homicide counts from 1979 to 2023, stratified by race, sex, age group, county urbanicity, and state, from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The firearm homicide surge periods 1985 to 1993 and 2014 to 2021 were analyzed. Although both Black and Hispanic people in the US bear a disproportionate burden of firearm homicide, Hispanic ethnicity was not consistently coded in mortality records over the study period (1979-2023); thus, a single categorization of Black or other race was used. Data analyses were conducted in April 2025 to September 2026. Exposure Presurge levels and presurge-to-surge changes in state measures of drug-market violence, proxy measures for firearm availability and use, economic strength, social or economic disadvantage, urban concentration, social or economic disruption, and policing capacity. Main Outcomes and Measures Annualized firearm homicide surge rates (deaths per 100 000 population, above presurge rates). Correlations between state-level surge rates and proxy measures were calculated. Results The 2014-2021 surge produced an estimated mean (SE) of 31 489 (509) firearm surge deaths, with a mean (SE) annualized rate of 1.20 (0.02) deaths per 100 000 population per year above presurge rates. In the 1985-1993 surge, the mean (SE) number of firearm surge deaths was 24 276 (580), with a mean (SE) annualized rate of 1.09 (0.03) deaths per 100 000 population. Both surges were driven entirely by firearm homicide, as non–firearm homicides declined over both periods. Deaths of young urban Black males (aged 15-24 years) accounted for 47% of 1985-1993 surge deaths but only 14% of the 2014-2021 surge. Compared with the 1985-1993 surge, during the 2014-2021 surge, the mean (SE) firearm homicide surge rates increased for females (0.15 [0.02] vs 0.38 [0.01]), people of races other than Black (0.22 [0.02] vs 0.48 [0.01]), and rural residents (0.13 [0.04] vs 0.83 [0.03]). Across US states, the 1985-1993 surge correlated with crack cocaine market activity ( r = 0.44; 95% CI, 0.19-0.64), while the 2014-2021 surge correlated with presurge firearm availability proxies ( r = 0.68 [95% CI, 0.50-0.81] for value of stolen firearms per capita) and COVID-19–related death rates ( r = 0.61; 95% CI, 0.40-0.76). Across both eras, higher state-level surge rates correlated with social or economic disadvantage, including premature mortality, poverty rates, lower employment, and household instability. Conclusions and Relevance In this serial cross-sectional study of US firearm homicide mortality, both the 2014-2021 surge, which was substantially larger and more demographically and geographically dispersed, and the 1985-1993 surge were associated with distinct proximal correlates but disproportionately affected states with broader structural vulnerabilities. Proximal drivers of rapid increases in homicide rates may exacerbate long-standing population vulnerabilities.

item.dc:creator: F. Vankee-Lin
Meishan Ai
Yuchuan Zhuang
Kathi L. Heffner
Dereck Salisbury
Danni Li
Clifford R. Jack
Fang Yu
item.description:
Authors: F. Vankee-Lin, Meishan Ai, Yuchuan Zhuang, Kathi L. Heffner, Dereck Salisbury, Danni Li, Clifford R. Jack, Fang Yu
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644426
Abstract: Importance Multicomponent lifestyle interventions show promise for promoting cognitive health, but their effects on clinically established brain aging markers among individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) are unclear. Intervention adherence may influence intervention efficacy. Objectives To evaluate the association of combined aerobic exercise and cognitive training (ACT) with brain aging markers and to explore the role of intervention adherence. Design, Setting, and Participants This secondary analysis of a phase 2, single-blind, 2 × 2 factorial randomized clinical trial with data collection lasting up to 18 months per participant was conducted at 3 academic research facilities between April 1, 2018, and July 17, 2024. Among 911 individuals screened, 146 participants with aMCI were randomized. Data were analyzed from October 10, 2025, to January 8, 2026. Interventions The ACT intervention was compared with 3 other intervention arms during a 6-month period, including speed-of-processing training (SOP), cycling, and mental leisure activities plus stretching (MS). Main Outcomes and Measures Alzheimer disease signature for cortical thickness (ADSCT) and natural log–transformed white matter hyperintensity (ln-WMH) were assessed at baseline, post intervention, and at the 12- and 18-month follow-ups. Outcome-specific modified intention-to-treat analyses used 100 forward-only multiple imputations and age-, sex-, and site-adjusted linear mixed-effects models with a participant random intercept. Visit-specific complete-case and attendance analyses used participants observed at baseline and the relevant follow-up. Results Among 146 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 73.8 [5.7] years), 75 (51.4%) were male. A total of 144 participants had baseline ADSCT and 141 had baseline ln-WMH measurements. In primary analyses, compared with ACT, SOP was associated with greater worsening in 18-month ADSCT change (B = −0.060 [95% CI, −0.117 to −0.004] mm; P = .04), and MS was associated with greater 12-month worsening (B = −0.066 [95% CI, −0.122 to −0.011] mm; P = .02). No primary ln-WMH contrast was significant. In visit-specific complete cases, cycling was associated with greater 18-month ln-WMH progression than ACT (B = 0.452 [95% CI, 0.131-0.772] natural log units; P = .006). Exploratory within-ACT analyses linked each of 10 additional sessions to greater postintervention ADSCT change (B = 0.022 [95% CI, 0.002-0.042] mm; P = .03), but not ln-WMH change. Conclusions and Relevance In this secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial of older adults with aMCI, ACT was associated with more favorable ADSCT change than SOP at 18 months and MS at 12 months. No primary ln-WMH contrast was significant. Attendance findings were post randomization and exploratory. Larger confirmatory trials are needed to verify these findings. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03313895

item.title: Timing of Antenatal Care, Stillbirth, and Infant Mortality in Migrant Mothers in Australia
item.dc:creator: Sadia Hossain
Ju-Lee Oei
Sithum Munasinghe
Marrwah Ahmadzai
Mithilesh Dronavalli
Andrew Page
item.description:
Authors: Sadia Hossain, Ju-Lee Oei, Sithum Munasinghe, Marrwah Ahmadzai, Mithilesh Dronavalli, Andrew Page
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644518
Abstract: Importance Timely antenatal care (ANC) reduces pregnancy risks, yet the association between delayed ANC and stillbirth or infant mortality among migrant mothers in Australia has not previously been investigated. Objective To examine whether delayed ANC is associated with higher stillbirth and infant mortality among Australia-born compared with migrant mothers. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study assessed births to non-Indigenous mothers in New South Wales from January 1, 2002, to December 31, 2020, followed up to infant age of 1 year. Mothers were categorized as Australia-born, migrant from English-speaking country (ESM), or migrant from non–English-speaking country (non-ESM). Data were analyzed between August 2025 and June 2026. Exposures Timing of first ANC, defined as 12 weeks or earlier, 13 to 19 weeks, 20 weeks or later, or no ANC. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcome was stillbirth (at ≥20 weeks) and infant mortality (at prehospital discharge, posthospital discharge, or 1 year). Adjusted relative risks (ARRs) were estimated using Poisson regression models, stratified by migration group. Results This study included 1 720 033 births (median [IQR] maternal age, 31.2 [27.4-34.8] years; 884 235 male infants [51.4%]), including 1 132 193 (65.8%) to Australia-born, 116 026 (6.7%) to ESM, and 471 814 (27.4%) to non-ESM mothers. Late ANC (&amp;gt;12 weeks) was more common in non-ESM mothers (190 338 [40.3%]) than Australia-born (334 790 [29.6%]) or ESM (41 029 [35.4%]) mothers. In cross-group comparisons, non-ESM mother status was associated with higher risk of adverse outcomes regardless of ANC timing. Compared with Australia-born mothers with early ANC (≤12 weeks), a higher risk of stillbirth (ARR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.18-1.33) and 1-year (ARR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.22-1.44), predischarge (ARR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.25-1.54), and postdischarge (ARR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.03-1.37) infant mortality was observed in non-ESM mothers accessing ANC by 12 weeks. Similar risk patterns were observed in non-ESM mothers with late ANC. In within-group comparisons, among Australia-born mothers, each category of delayed ANC was associated with higher risk. No ANC was associated with the highest risks across all maternal groups for stillbirth and 1-year infant mortality. For non-ESM mothers, late ANC (≥20 weeks) was associated with a lower risk of predischarge mortality (ARR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.61-0.92) but a higher risk of postdischarge mortality (ARR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.02-1.65). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 1.72 million births, higher risks of stillbirths and infant mortalities were observed in non-ESM mothers regardless of ANC timing, warranting further investigation.

item.title: Clinician Acceptance of Large Language Model–Generated Discharge Summaries
item.dc:creator: Kathleen Goldsmith
Maite Arribas
Fidan Damirova
Mazin Mukhaiber
Ghavin Kuganesan
Subanki Srisakthivel
Seham Shaffee
Hutan Momtazian
item.description:
Authors: Kathleen Goldsmith, Maite Arribas, Fidan Damirova, Mazin Mukhaiber, Ghavin Kuganesan, Subanki Srisakthivel, Seham Shaffee, Hutan Momtazian, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644496
Abstract: Importance Hospital discharge summaries are essential for continuity of care, but fragmented electronic health record (EHR) data can compromise their quality and safety. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for clinical documentation tasks despite limited evidence regarding their performance in health care settings compared with the current standard of care. Objective To evaluate clinician acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries derived from EHRs compared with routine clinician-written summaries. Design, Setting, and Participants In this retrospective comparative effectiveness study using a prespecified noninferiority framework, acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries was compared with clinician-authored discharge summaries. Admission records from 5 London hospitals for September 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, were evaluated against the full admission record by practicing physicians. Admissions were eligible only if the clinician-authored discharge summary contained identifiable clinical summary, plan and requested actions, and information given sections. Data analysis was conducted from July 2025 to February 2026. Intervention LLM-generated summaries were produced using GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI) and a clinician-codesigned prompt. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was clinician signoff with no or minor edits, derived from 2 sequential questions: (1) whether the reviewer would sign the summary and (2) whether no, minor, or major edits were required. A 5–percentage-point noninferiority margin was prespecified. Secondary outcomes assessed accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, poor; 2, fair; 3, good; 4, very good; and 5, excellent) and potential harmfulness of missing or incorrect information (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, no harm; 2, minor harm; 3, moderate harm; 4, high harm; and 5, extremely high harm). Results The study sample included 1294 (649 clinician-authored and 645 LLM-generated) unique case discharge summaries that were evaluated against the full admission record by 12 practicing physicians. Case patients had a median age of 46.0 years (IQR, 26.2-69.8 years), 733 (56.6%) were assigned female at birth, and the median length of stay was 3.0 days (IQR, 1.0-7.0 days). The absolute difference in model-estimated probability of signoff with no or minor edits (LLM generated minus clinician authored) was 22.2 percentage points (95% CI, 19.0-27.5 percentage points); the lower bound exceeded the prespecified noninferiority margin of −5 percentage points, demonstrating noninferiority. LLM-generated summaries received higher ratings for accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (adjusted risk differences for scores ≥4 ranged from 19.4 [95% CI, 14.8-24.1] to 29.1 [95% CI, 25.1-33.6] percentage points; all 95% CIs excluded 0). LLM-generated summaries also had a lower proportion of cases rated 3 or greater for potential harm on the clinical summary and plan and requested actions sections (140 of 534 [26.2%] and 124 of 462 [26.8%]) compared with clinician-authored summaries (271 of 601 [45.1%] and 278 of 540 [51.5%]). Conclusions and Relevance In this study, LLM-generated discharge summaries met the current standard of care, representing a promising early use case for generative artificial intelligence in health care with close clinician oversight.

item.dc:creator: Yael Paz
Deiriai Myers
Kate Wisniewski
Nicole M. Henry

Barbara H. Chaiyachati

item.description:
Authors: Yael Paz, Deiriai Myers, Kate Wisniewski, Nicole M. Henry, Sara L. Kornfield, Barbara H. Chaiyachati, Lauren K. White, Florence Momplaisir, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644526
Abstract: Importance Neighborhood deprivation is an important environmental context for understanding child development and has been linked in extensive prior work with physical and cognitive outcomes. However, neighborhood deprivation is understudied in relation to socioemotional development in early childhood, a critical period for prevention and intervention. Objective To examine prospective associations between neighborhood deprivation and children’s socioemotional development from infancy to preschool age and to test whether associations differ by race. Design, Setting, and Participants In this longitudinal cohort study, participants were mother-child dyads with available neighborhood and socioemotional assessment data who were recruited in April 2020 from the greater Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, area as part of a longitudinal cohort within a large health system. Assessments were conducted at child ages 1, 2, and 4 years. Data collection started in June 2021 for children aged 1 year and in May 2024 for children aged 4 years and ended in March 2025. Exposure A composite neighborhood deprivation index derived from objective US census–based measures linked to participants’ residential addresses, including the Child Opportunity Index, Area Deprivation Index, Social Vulnerability Index, and Heat Vulnerability Index. Main Outcomes and Measures Parent-reported developmental concerns from Ages and Stages Questionnaires: Social-Emotional, Second Edition (ASQ:SE-2) scores at each age and electronic health record (EHR) data on developmental or behavioral diagnoses. Results The analytic sample included 249 mother-child dyads; 125 children (50.2%) were female. A total of 130 households (52.2%) were included in the White group and 118 (47.8%) in the Black or multiracial group. Greater neighborhood deprivation was associated with more parent-reported socioemotional concerns (β = 0.29 [95% CI, 0.20-0.38]; P &amp;lt; .001), independent of family income and maternal anxiety. Children from more deprived neighborhoods had increased odds of being referred for monitoring or intervention (odds ratio [OR], 2.43 [95% CI, 1.05-5.64]; P = .04). A similar pattern was observed for developmental or behavioral diagnoses in children's electronic health records (OR, 1.40 [95% CI, 1.01-2.01]; P = .050). The magnitude of these associations was greater among children from Black or multiracial households, who lived in significantly more deprived neighborhoods than children from White households (χ 2 1 = 304.62; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, neighborhood deprivation was associated with worse socioemotional functioning across early childhood, above and beyond family-level factors. Children from Black or multiracial compared with White households lived in neighborhoods with greater disadvantage, emphasizing underlying structural inequities and the importance of community-level investment and equitable urban planning to support early developmental health and equity.

item.title: Sudden Deaths From Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Proximity to Neurosurgical Tertiary Care
item.dc:creator: Aleksanteri Asikainen
Miikka Korja
Jaakko Kaprio
Anna Ranta
Derrick Bennett
Amanda G. Thrift
P. Alan Barber
Suzanne Barker-Collo
item.description:
Authors: Aleksanteri Asikainen, Miikka Korja, Jaakko Kaprio, Anna Ranta, Derrick Bennett, Amanda G. Thrift, P. Alan Barber, Suzanne Barker-Collo, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644245
Abstract: Importance A substantial proportion of deaths due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) occur without admission to neurosurgical units. Whether this proportion varies by geographic region is unclear. Objective To determine the proportion of SAH deaths without neurosurgical unit admission across hospital districts in 2 high-income countries. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective, population-based cohort study used 2 externally validated nationwide administrative data collections in all 41 hospital districts and 10 neurosurgical units in Finland and New Zealand from January 1, 2001, to December 31, 2017. Participants included all hospitalized and fatal nonhospitalized cases with SAH. Data were analyzed from July 1, 2024, to September 7, 2026. Exposures Hospital district of residence and its distance to the designated neurosurgical referral center, grouped into 4 zones. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the death-based proportion of all 30-day deaths after SAH that occurred without neurosurgical unit admission (prehospital deaths plus deaths within 30 days after admission to a nonneurosurgical unit divided by all 30-day deaths from SAH). This proportion was estimated across 41 hospital districts and demographic groups, with age- and sex-adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and 95% CIs. Results A total of 12 912 patients with SAH (7856 in Finland and 5056 in New Zealand; median age, 58 [IQR, 49-69] years; 7924 [61.4%] women) were included. Of all 5418 SAH deaths, 3819 (70.5%) occurred without neurosurgical unit admission: 2203 of 3114 (70.7%) in Finland (interdistrict range, 403 of 644 [62.6%] to 5 of 5 [100%]) and 1616 of 2304 (70.1%) in New Zealand (interdistrict range, 111 of 190 [58.4%] to 22 of 23 [95.7%]). Compared with districts containing a neurosurgical unit (1723 of 2602 [66.2%]), the death-based proportions were higher in close-distance (1-130 km; 796 of 1129 [70.5%]; RR, 1.07 [95% CI, 1.02-1.12]), middle-distance (131-157 km; 469 of 599 [78.3%]; RR, 1.18 [95% CI, 1.12-1.24]), and far-distance (158-371 km; 831 of 1088 [76.4%]; RR, 1.15 [95% CI, 1.10-1.20]) zones. This proportion increased by 6.7% (95% CI, 4.9%-8.5%) for each additional 100 km to a neurosurgical unit. The proportions decreased in both countries over time. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 12 912 patients with SAH, most deaths occurred without neurosurgical unit admission, and this proportion increased with distance to the neurosurgical referral center. Prevention and early management outside tertiary care may therefore warrant priority in reducing SAH mortality.

item.title: Resistance Exercise Training for Depressive Symptoms
item.dc:creator: Darragh O’Sullivan
Jennifer M. Rice
Jacob D. Meyer
Seana Smith
Brett R. Gordon
Cillian McDowell
Ian Sherwin
Mark Lyons
item.description:
Authors: Darragh O’Sullivan, Jennifer M. Rice, Jacob D. Meyer, Seana Smith, Brett R. Gordon, Cillian McDowell, Ian Sherwin, Mark Lyons, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644254
Abstract: Importance Resistance exercise training (RET) has established antidepressant effects compared with inactive control conditions; however, its effects vs active comparisons remain unclear. Objective To quantify the association of RET efficacy with active and inactive comparisons for depressive symptoms and explore variability across moderators. Data Sources Published articles were identified using Google Scholar, MEDLINE, PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycInfo from inception to July 7, 2025. Study Selection Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) with at least 3 weeks of RET or any non-RET comparison and a validated depressive symptom measure at baseline and at least 3 weeks were included. Active comparisons were aerobic exercise training, relaxation, flexibility, mind-body exercise, nutrition, education, advice or attention, mixed activities, and balance exercises. Inactive comparisons were no treatment, waiting lists, and continued usual care. Data Extraction and Synthesis Three reviewers independently extracted data. Meta-regression was used to test moderators, including primary moderators (age, sex, mental health status, RET duration, intensity, concealed allocation). Study quality was assessed using a modified Detsky scale. Main Outcomes and Measures All available associations of RET vs comparison conditions with depressive symptoms were quantified from baseline to at least 3 weeks. Random-effects models were used. Results Across 80 RCTs including 6123 participants (2880 participants [47.0%] in RET groups and 3243 [53.0%] in non-RET comparison groups; mean [SD] age, 57 [16] years; 3412 female [67.1%]), the number of effect sizes examined was 176; 57 RCTs enrolled participants with an illness. Resistance exercise training was associated with a significant, heterogenous, small-magnitude antidepressant effect size (Δ = 0.32 [95% CI, 0.25-0.39]; z = 9.31; P &amp;lt; .001) across all comparisons. The effect size was larger vs inactive comparisons (Δ = 0.54 [95% CI, 0.39-0.68]; z = 7.22; P &amp;lt; .001) than active comparisons (Δ = 0.21 [95% CI, 0.14-0.27]; z = 6.20; P &amp;lt; .001). Versus active comparisons, RET was associated with a significant, heterogenous, small-magnitude antidepressant effect size, with larger effect sizes among participants with a mental illness (Δ = 0.40 [95% CI, 0.29-0.50]) vs without a mental illness (Δ = 0.11 [95% CI, 0.04-0.18]). Versus inactive comparisons, RET was associated with a significant, heterogenous, moderate-magnitude antidepressant effect size, with larger effect sizes for all-female cohorts (Δ = 0.87 [95% CI, 0.60-1.14]), RET frequencies of at least 4 days per week (Δ = 0.46 [95% CI, 0.31-0.60]), and session durations of 30 minutes or less (Δ = 1.75 [95% CI, 0.97-2.54]), and smaller effect sizes with concealed allocation (Δ = 0.32 [95% CI, 0.20-0.44]). Conclusions and Relevance This meta-analysis and meta-regression analysis found that RET was associated with moderate-magnitude, clinically meaningful reductions in depressive symptoms that were greater than other activities with antidepressant benefits, supporting the recommendation of RET in the treatment of depression.

item.title: Neighborhood Exposure to Firearm Violence and Measures of Psychosocial Distress
item.dc:creator: James Macinko
Tanvi Shinkre
Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi
Jack Kappelman
Diana Silver
item.description:
Authors: James Macinko, Tanvi Shinkre, Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi, Jack Kappelman, Diana Silver
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644237
Abstract: Importance Exposure to firearm violence is believed to have substantial indirect health effects among those who experience and witness it. Objective To assess whether neighborhood firearm violence is associated with psychological and behavioral outcomes. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study links geocoded, individual-level data from adults participating in the 2021 and 2022 California Health Interview Surveys, a state-representative survey conducted annually by the UCLA Center for Health Policy Research linked to shooting events near interviewees’ home from the Gun Violence Archive. Data analysis was performed from August to October 2025. Exposure Any shooting event occurring within 500 m of interviewees’ households within the past 12 months (January 1, 2020, and December 31, 2022). Sensitivity analyses included any fatal shooting, any shooting within the past 2 months, and more than 1 shooting event. Main Outcome and Measures Primary outcomes were self-reported worry about experiencing firearm violence, feeling unsafe in one’s neighborhood, heavy substance use, and psychological distress. Survey-adjusted multivariable Poisson regression models assessed the association between the exposure and each outcome. Results Among the 45 916 adults interviewed (mean [SD] age, 48.2 [18.7] years; 26 077 [51.8%] female), 6289 (17.2%, weighted) had a shooting occur near their home; there were no missing data. Polysubstance use was positively associated with most exposures, with the highest incident rate ratios (IRRs) among those experiencing a recent shooting in their neighborhood within the past 2 months (IRR, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.18-1.68) and those experiencing more than 1 shooting (IRR, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.14-1.55). The highest magnitude associations for each exposure were observed with the outcome of feeling unsafe in one’s neighborhood among those experiencing a recent shooting event (IRR, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.52-1.97) or more than 1 shooting (IRR, 2.36; 95% CI, 2.17-2.56). All exposures had a positive association with worry about experiencing firearm violence, with IRRs of 1.14 (95% CI, 1.04-1.24) for those experiencing any shooting to 1.28 (95% CI, 1.13-1.43) for those experiencing more than 1 shooting in the past 12 months. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of the association between firearm violence and self-reported psychosocial distress, exposure to neighborhood firearm violence was associated with a range of outcomes that may affect people’s perceptions of their safety and could potentially contribute to negative coping behaviors, such as substance use.

item.title: Climate Vulnerability, Historical Redlining, and Children’s Mental Health Care Use
item.dc:creator: Eun Kyung Lee
Megan B. Cole
Sugy Choi
item.description:
Authors: Eun Kyung Lee, Megan B. Cole, Sugy Choi
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2645085
Abstract: Importance Structural inequities stemming from historical redlining and environmental injustice have created varying levels of risk among marginalized communities. However, the association of climate risk and structural racism with pediatric mental health care use remains underexplored. Objectives To examine associations between climate vulnerability and pediatric mental health care use, and to assess whether these associations vary by historical redlining status. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study of children aged younger than 18 years residing in New York State between 2017 and 2022 used all-payer hospital administrative data from the New York State Department of Health. Statistical analysis was conducted from January 2025 through February 2026. Main Outcome and Measures Outcomes included mental health–related emergency department (ED) and outpatient visits identified using International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision –coded mental health diagnosis subtypes (eg, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), aggregated at the census-tract level. The primary exposure was climate-specific Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles (where 1 indicates low climate vulnerability and 4 indicates high climate vulnerability). Poisson regression models were conducted to examine associations between Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles and mental health–related health care utilization, including interactions with neighborhood-level redlining status (Home Owners’ Loan Corporation grades C/D vs A/B) and subtype-specific analyses. Models adjusted for age, sex, self- or guardian-reported race and ethnicity, and neighborhood-level covariates, with coefficients reported as rate ratios (RRs). Results A total of 553 134 mental health–related visits were included (mean [SD] age, 7.2 [5.8] years; 285 526 male [51.6%]). Compared with children living in areas with the lowest climate vulnerability, those living in the highest-vulnerability areas had higher outpatient visit rates (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.72-2.27) and non–statistically significantly higher ED visit rates (RR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.96-1.35). Associations between high climate vulnerability and mental health–related health care utilization varied by redlining status. In historically redlined neighborhoods, high climate vulnerability was associated with outpatient health care utilization (RR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.44-1.51; P &amp;lt; .001 for interaction) and, to a lesser extent, ED utilization (RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.09; P &amp;lt; .001 for interaction); in nonredlined neighborhoods high climate vulnerability was associated with lower outpatient health care utilization (RR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.45-0.49; P &amp;lt; .001 for interaction) and not associated with ED utilization (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.93-1.07). Associations also varied across mental health diagnosis subtypes, with higher climate vulnerability associated with increased health care utilization for most diagnosis subtypes. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of children, residence in historically redlined and climate-vulnerable neighborhoods was associated with higher rates of mental health–related health care utilization. These findings highlight geographic patterns in mental health–related health care utilization that may be relevant to future research on climate preparedness, mental health services, culturally responsive care, and access to services for children experiencing climate-related stressors and structural inequities.

item.title: Multilevel Mobility Intervention and Life-Space Mobility in Older Hospitalized Medical Patients
item.dc:creator: Leon Schiffmann
Pascal Leist
Lisa Marti
Livia Bee
Julia I. Beck
Leandra Pfisterer
Eric Geissbühler
Filippa L. M. Kühni
item.description:
Authors: Leon Schiffmann, Pascal Leist, Lisa Marti, Livia Bee, Julia I. Beck, Leandra Pfisterer, Eric Geissbühler, Filippa L. M. Kühni, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643903
Abstract: Importance Low mobility is common during an acute hospitalization and is associated with adverse outcomes, such as loss of independence and death. Previous interventions that were successful in increasing hospital mobility required resources that are not available in everyday clinical practice, limiting their scalability. Objective To assess whether the theory-informed Intervention to Increase Mobility in Older Hospitalized Medical Patients (INTOMOB) improves life-space mobility at 30 days in older hospitalized medical patients. Design, Setting, and Participants This is a multicenter, parallel, partially blinded, cluster randomized clinical superiority trial, with randomization at the hospital ward level and 180-day follow-up. Patients were recruited between October 2023 and January 2025 at acute general internal medicine wards of 3 Swiss hospitals. Main eligibility criteria were age 60 years or older, living in the community, and planned hospital stay 3 or more days. Intervention The intervention was compared with standard of care and included booklets and videos for patients, health care professional training, and posters in the wards. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was life-space mobility at 30 days, a measure of how far and often a person moves within their environment, from bedroom to beyond their town (range, 0-120 points, with higher scores denoting greater mobility). Secondary outcomes included physical activity during hospitalization, new institutionalizations (ie, transition to nursing home), and quality of life. For time-to-event outcomes, Cox models with cluster-robust SEs were used. Multinomial logistic regression with robust SEs was used for categorical outcomes. Results Of 1334 eligible patients, 383 (median [IQR] age, 75 [68 to 81] years; 234 male [61.1%]) agreed to participate and were randomized to 12 clusters (183 patients [47.8%] in the intervention group and 200 patients [52.2%] in the control group). The primary outcome was available for 327 patients (85.4%). The median (IQR) length of stay was 5 (3 to 7) days. Life-space mobility at 30 days was not significantly different between control and intervention groups (adjusted difference, 0.67 points; 95% CI, −4.35 to 5.68 points). There were no serious adverse events potentially related to the intervention. There was no consistent statistically significant difference in any other secondary outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance The INTOMOB intervention did not result in a significantly improved short-term life-space mobility or other clinical outcomes. However, the feasibility of the INTOMOB intervention provides a foundation for future mobility interventions aiming to improve both effectiveness and applicability in everyday clinical practice. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05639231 ; Swiss National Clinical Trial Portal Identifier: SNCTP000005259

item.title: Study Rationale, Enrollment Characteristics, and Central Review of Clinical Stage
item.dc:creator: Parminder Singh
Melissa Plets
Jason Efsthathiou
Sameer G. Jhavar
Catherine Tangen
Scott Delacroix
Carie Marquette
Kent W. Mouw
item.description:
Authors: Parminder Singh, Melissa Plets, Jason Efsthathiou, Sameer G. Jhavar, Catherine Tangen, Scott Delacroix, Carie Marquette, Kent W. Mouw, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644122
Abstract: Importance Trimodality therapy (TMT) is an established bladder-preservation approach for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). Accurate clinical staging remains challenging and may affect patient selection, trial design, and interpretation of outcomes. Objective To describe the design, accrual, and baseline characteristics of the Phase III Randomized Trial of Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy With or Without Atezolizumab in Localized Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (INTACT) trial and evaluate agreement between site-reported and centrally reviewed clinical stage and the prevalence of high-risk disease features. Design, Setting, and Participants INTACT is a phase 3 randomized clinical trial that enrolled patients with localized MIBC (stage cT2-T4aN0M0) at 136 US sites between April 2019 and March 2025. For this analysis, 243 patients with available source documentation were randomly selected by the SWOG Statistical Center for central clinical staging review. Interventions Patients were randomized to physician’s choice of concurrent chemotherapy (cisplatin, gemcitabine, or 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin C) and radiotherapy (bladder only or small pelvis; 64-64.8 Gy), with or without atezolizumab (1200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks for 9 cycles). Main Outcomes and Measures The trial’s primary end point is 3-year bladder-intact event-free survival, which is not reported in this analysis. Outcomes for the present analysis included trial accrual, clinical stage distribution, agreement between site-reported stage and the initial independent central reviewer, and prevalence of predefined high-risk features (carcinoma in situ, unilateral hydronephrosis, or tumor &amp;gt;5 cm). Agreement was assessed using Cohen κ and directional disagreement using the McNemar test. Results Among 485 randomized patients, the median (IQR) age was 73.8 (37.6-93.6) years, 384 (79.2%) were male, 16 (3.3%) were Asian, 33 (6.8%) were Black, and 419 (86.4%) were White. Site investigators classified 398 (82.1%) as stage cT2 and 87 (17.9%) as stage cT3 or T4a. Among 243 patients selected for central review, 201 (82.7%) had site-reported stage cT2 disease and 42 (17.3%) had stage cT3 or T4a disease. Agreement between site-reported stage and the initial independent central reviewer was moderate (κ = 0.48; 95% CI, 0.34-0.62). Of 201 site-reported stage cT2 cases, 24 (11.9%) were assigned stage cT3 or T4a by the central reviewer; of 42 site-reported stage cT3 or T4a cases, 15 (35.7%) were assigned stage cT2. Among patients with site-reported stage cT2 disease, 113 (56.2%) had at least 1 high-risk feature. Overall, 155 of 243 patients (63.8%) had at least 1 high-risk feature. Conclusions and Relevance In this phase 3 randomized clinical trial, a pragmatic design facilitated accrual of 485 patients to a US bladder-preservation trial. Clinical staging showed moderate agreement between site investigators and independent central review, and more than half of patients classified as stage cT2 had additional high-risk features. These findings support standardized collection of clinical staging and high-risk disease characteristics in future bladder-preservation trials. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03775265

item.description:
Authors: Koji Matsuo, Naoko Komura, Aoi Yamaguchi, Yurika Arakaki, Shinya Matsuzaki, Nikita A. Rao, Nandita Ramkumar, Matthew W. Lee, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644168
Abstract: Importance Cancer survivors are individuals with a diagnosis of malignant neoplasm, either living with (ie, current cancer survivors) or free of (ie, past cancer survivors) cancer. As the prevalence of cancer survivors of reproductive age increases worldwide, assessment of pregnancy characteristics and outcomes among past cancer survivors is important. Objective To assess the temporal trends, clinical and obstetric characteristics, and maternal morbidity at delivery among current and past cancer survivors. Design, Setting, and Participants This nationwide cross-sectional study used National Inpatient Sample data for hospital deliveries from 2016 to 2023. Analyses were conducted from April to May 2026. Exposure A prior or current diagnosis of cancer at hospital delivery, with individuals classified as being a past cancer survivor, a current cancer survivor, or an individual without a cancer diagnosis. Main Outcome and Measure The primary outcome was severe maternal morbidity at delivery, assessed with multivariable generalized linear models with a Poisson distribution. Results Among 28 360 443 hospital deliveries, there were 106 740 (0.4%) hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors, 21 975 (&amp;lt;0.1%) for current cancer survivors, and 28 231 728 (99.5%) without a cancer diagnosis. The median (IQR) maternal age at delivery was 33 (29-36), 32 (27-36), and 29 (25-33) years among past cancer survivors, current cancer survivors, and individuals without a cancer diagnosis, respectively. During the 8-year study period, hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors increased from 30.1 to 45.6 per 10 000 hospital deliveries (average annual percentage change [AAPC] = 6.3% [95% CI, 5.1%-7.9%]), whereas hospital deliveries for current cancer survivors were unchanged (7.0 to 7.4 per 10 000 hospital deliveries; AAPC = 0.2% [95% CI, −2.8% to 3.7%]). Most hospital deliveries (57.6%) for past cancer survivors were full-term, whereas only 39.6% were full-term for current cancer survivors. Compared with the no cancer group, the severe maternal morbidity rate was higher for the past cancer survivor group (11.9 vs 6.8 per 1000 hospital deliveries; adjusted incidence rate ratio [IRR], 1.45 [95% CI, 1.37-1.53]) and for the current cancer survivor group (48.2 vs 6.8 per 1000 hospital deliveries; adjusted IRR, 3.80 [95% CI, 3.58-4.04]), including the inpatient maternal mortality rate during the hospital delivery admission (273.0 vs 7.0 per 100 000 hospital deliveries; adjusted IRR, 14.24 [95% CI, 10.87-18.66]). Conclusions and Relevance In this US cross-sectional study, the prevalence of hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors increased from 2016 to 2023, and severe maternal morbidity was increased at delivery for past and current cancer survivors. These findings support the importance of preconception evaluation for cancer survivors and early referral to tertiary care centers with multidisciplinary teams, as currently recommended by multiple organizations.

item.title: Work Hours, Emergency Department Context, and Workplace Violence Among Nurses
item.dc:creator: Lindsay Thompson Munn
Nathaniel Sean O’Connell
Carolyn S. Huffman

item.description:
Authors: Lindsay Thompson Munn, Nathaniel Sean O’Connell, Carolyn S. Huffman, Esita Patel, Kristie L. Foley, Cheryl B. Jones, Jason P. Stopyra
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644016
Abstract: Importance Workplace violence is common in high-risk health care settings, with consequences for clinician well-being and care delivery. Less is known about multilevel work-system factors associated with workplace violence in emergency department (ED) nurses. Objective To characterize workplace violence among ED nurses and identify multilevel work-system factors associated with workplace violence. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study used nurse survey data combined with administrative and electronic medical record data collected in 2023 from nurses working in 11 EDs in a multisite health system in the southeastern US. Exposure Multilevel work-system factors, with primary exposures of interest including overtime, shift type, and ED type (freestanding vs in-hospital); additional covariates included individual, team, and ED-level characteristics. Main Outcomes and Measures Any self-reported workplace violence in the prior month (threats, physical violence, verbal abuse, unwanted sexual attention, or bullying) from patients, visitors, and/or coworkers. Associations were estimated using mixed-effects logistic regression with a random intercept for emergency department site and factor selection using cross-validated least absolute shrinkage and selectrion operator regression. Nurses in the supplemental staffing team were excluded from this analysis. Results Among 337 ED nurses (mean [SD] age, 34.9 [9.5] years; 289 [85.8%] female; 287 [85.2% white; mean [SD] nursing experience, 9.0 [8.2] years), 296 (87.8%) reported workplace violence in the prior month. Incidents of WPV involved patients or visitors (292 of 296 [98.6%]) and coworkers (60 of 296 [20.3%]). In adjusted mixed-effects models (n = 299), overtime was associated with higher odds of workplace violence (OR, 3.21; 95% CI, 1.30-7.93), while night shift (OR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.10-0.78) and employment in a freestanding ED (OR, 0.25; 95% CI, 0.09-0.76) were associated with lower odds. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of ED nurses, workplace violence was common and was associated with overtime and ED context. These findings support further evaluation of work-hour practices and context-specific approaches to workplace violence prevention.

Authors: Teresa Macarulla, Vincent Picozzi, Sreenivasa R. Chandana, Bohuslav Melichar, Anup Kasi, Jin Gang, Javier Gallego, Christelle de la Fouchardière, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641241
Abstract: Importance The PANOVA-3 trial demonstrated the survival benefit and tolerability of Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, but understanding the impact of TTFields therapy on quality of life (QoL) and pain is important for clinical decision-making. Objective To analyze the impact of TTFields therapy concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel on QoL and pain outcomes using prospective data from PANOVA-3. Design, Setting, and Participants This is a prespecified secondary analysis of PANOVA-3, which was a global, open-label, multicenter, phase 3 randomized clinical trial in adult patients with previously untreated locally advanced unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma (LA-PAC). A total of 571 patients were randomized between May 1, 2018, and March 31, 2023, with follow-up completed October 31, 2024. Data analysis was performed from November 2024 to May 2025. Intervention Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive either TTFields therapy (150 kHz) with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel or gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. Nab-paclitaxel (125 mg/m 2 ) and gemcitabine (1000 mg/m 2 ) were administered intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of 28-day cycles. Duration of follow-up was 18 months. Main Outcomes and Measures QoL was measured using the European Organization for the Research and Treatment of Cancer Core Quality of Life Questionnaire and the 26-item pancreatic cancer module. End points were mean changes from baseline QoL scores, deterioration-free survival of QoL, and time to opioid use. An analysis of pain medication use was performed post hoc. Results At baseline, 562 patients (median [IQR] age, 67 [31-90] years; 295 [52.5%] female), including 279 of 285 patients in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm and 283 of 286 patients in the gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm, completed the EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaire. Global health status was stable during the 26-month follow-up in both study arms. Digestive symptoms, pain, and pancreatic pain were improved from 2 months after treatment initiation throughout treatment and follow-up in the TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel arm. TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel was associated with longer deterioration-free survival for global health status than gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone (median [IQR], 7.1 [3.5-14.8] vs 5.7 [2.3-11.5] months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.77; 95% CI, 0.61-0.97; P = .02). Longer deterioration-free survival was also observed for most items on the digestive symptoms scales (indigestion and altered bowel habit were similar between the 2 arms). Median (IQR) deterioration-free survival was significantly longer with TTFields plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel for pain (10.1 [4.0-20.9] vs 7.4 [3.5-14.5] months; HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.54-0.89; P = .003) and pancreatic pain (14.7 [6.2-46.2] vs 10.2 [5.6-18.2] months; HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.52-0.90; P = .006) as was median time to opioid use in the modified intention-to-treat population (9.3 [3.9-18.6] vs 6.7 [1.1-16.3] months; HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.55-0.93; P = .01). Conclusions and Relevance This secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that TTFields therapy with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel improved QoL and provided clinically meaningful benefits in pain outcomes compared with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel alone. This study’s results suggest that TTFields therapy with gemicitabine and nab-paclitaxel is practice-changing for patients with unresectable LA-PAC. item.description:
Authors: Molly O. Hunter, Kyulim Lee, Raul E. Sanchez, Isaac Kistler, Charles A. Elmaraghy, Amy M. Manning, Prasanth Pattisapu, Tendy Chiang, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643915
Abstract: Importance Diagnosis and treatment of ankyloglossia has increased in recent years. A lack of universal evaluation and management guidelines may contribute to inconsistent practice patterns and variable access to care. Objective To evaluate access to care and practice pattern variation in the treatment of ankyloglossia as a source of breastfeeding difficulty across clinicians and sites of care in Ohio. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study of pediatric dentists and pediatric and general otolaryngologists providing treatment to pediatric patients in Ohio was conducted using a secret shopper approach from October 6, 2025, to January 5, 2026. All pediatric dentists and otolaryngologists providing treatment to pediatric patients were eligible for inclusion. Health care professionals were identified using lists obtained from the Ohio State Dental Board and the American Academy of Otolaryngology. Exposure Clinics were contacted via phone by a simulated patient’s mother using a vignette describing a 2-week-old infant with breastfeeding difficulty characterized by painful latch and inquiring regarding ankyloglossia (ie, tongue tie) evaluation. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were time to first available appointment and procedure cost to patient on the day of service. Secondary outcomes included referral requirement, potential for same-day procedures, procedure technique, additional procedures discussed during scheduling, insurance acceptance, and total cost of consultation and procedure. Results A total of 175 clinics representing 487 health care professionals (299 dentists and 188 otolaryngologists) were contacted. The median (IQR) appointment wait time was 14 (7-28) days. For practices providing cost information, time-of-service cash payment was required by 31 of 36 dental offices (86%), while all otolaryngology practices (38 of 38; [100%]) billed medical insurance. Dental clinics were more likely to empirically recommend other procedures (eg, maxillary frenulum release) at the time of appointment scheduling (29 of 45 [64%]) than otolaryngology offices (1 of 38 [3%]) ( P &amp;lt; .001). Across all practices, the median (IQR) cost of lingual frenotomy alone was $474 ($350-$545), while total cost (consultation and all recommended procedures) ranged from $200 to $1515. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of pediatric dental and otolaryngology clinics in Ohio, access to care for ankyloglossia was similar, but the anticipated cost of procedures varied widely, as did empiric recommendations for intervention beyond lingual frenotomy. Prospective patients should be aware of this heterogeneity and the potential for significant price differences for treatment.

item.title: Body Mass Index Peak-Rebound Patterns and Inhibitory Control Among Young Children
item.dc:creator: Jamil M. Lane
Izzuddin M. Aris
Hsiao-Hsien Leon Hsu
Emily Oken
Vishal Midya
Rosalind J. Wright
Daniel N. Klein
María Del Carmen Hernández-Chávez
item.description:
Authors: Jamil M. Lane, Izzuddin M. Aris, Hsiao-Hsien Leon Hsu, Emily Oken, Vishal Midya, Rosalind J. Wright, Daniel N. Klein, María Del Carmen Hernández-Chávez, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642834
Abstract: Importance Childhood obesity has been linked with poor inhibitory control, and atypical body mass index (BMI) growth trajectories may identify children at higher risk for poor inhibitory control. Inhibitory control is also sexually dimorphic (male vs female), as maladaptive inhibitory control is more common in males. Objective To investigate the association between early childhood BMI peak-rebound patterns and inhibitory control development at 4 to 5 and 6 to 7 years and test whether there is a sexually dimorphic association. Design, Setting, and Participants The Programming Research in Obesity, Growth, Environment, and Social Stressors study is a prebirth cohort that recruited pregnant women receiving prenatal care through the Mexican Social Security Institute from July 2007 to February 2010 and followed up from pregnancy through age 8 years. Data were analyzed from November 2024 to December 2025. Exposure Repeated weight and length or height measurements were collected from birth to 8 years and mixed-effects models were used to characterize sex- and child-specific BMI trajectories and derive age and magnitude of the BMI peak (maximum inflection point during infancy) and rebound (minimum inflection point during early childhood). Main Outcomes and Measures Children completed the Conners Kiddie Continuous Performance Test, second edition, to assess inhibitory control at ages 4 to 5 and 6 to 7 years, and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess associations of age and magnitude of BMI peak and rebound with inhibitory control across the 2 time points. Sex-specific trajectories were evaluated by modeling interactions between child sex. Results Among 539 children included in the study, 278 (51.6%) were male; 277 (51.4%) were born to mothers with low socioeconomic status, and the mean (SD) gestational age at birth was 38.4 (1.6) weeks. After adjusting for covariates, a 1-SD higher BMI at peak was associated with higher T-scores for hit reaction time standard errors (β = 0.89; 95% CI, 0.20 to 1.58). A 1-SD higher age at rebound was associated with higher hit reaction time (β = 2.35; 95% CI, −0.01 to 4.72). However, age at peak and BMI at rebound were not associated with any inhibitory control measure. Children with early timing of peak and rebound exhibited higher T-scores for omission errors (β = 4.05; 95% CI, 0.96 to 7.13), while children with early timing of peak and late timing of BMI rebound had lower T-scores for hit reaction time (β = −4.16; 95% CI, −7.29 to −1.02) compared with those with normal timing of peak and rebound. In males, both older age and a higher magnitude of BMI rebound were associated with lower omission error T-scores, whereas in females, variations in age and magnitude of BMI patterns were associated with higher T-scores for hit reaction time and hit reaction time standard errors. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 539 children in Mexico, early-life BMI peak-rebound trajectories across childhood were associated with inhibitory control. These findings extend the literature beyond the well-established effects of BMI peak-rebound on metabolic conditions.

item.title: Neighborhood Exposome at Birth and Trajectories of Epigenetic Age Acceleration Across Childhood
item.dc:creator: Qingyue E. Yuan
Anne K. Bozack
Vincent Paquin
Sarina Abrishamcar
Ella J. Arrant
Ying Xu
Sheryl L. Rifas-Shiman

item.description:
Authors: Qingyue E. Yuan, Anne K. Bozack, Vincent Paquin, Sarina Abrishamcar, Ella J. Arrant, Ying Xu, Sheryl L. Rifas-Shiman, Yinxian Chen, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644321
Abstract: Importance Epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) has been linked to increased disease risk in adults, yet its developmental trajectories and early-life neighborhood determinants remain poorly understood. Objective To examine whether there are associations between the neighborhood exposome at birth and EAA trajectories from early childhood through adolescence. Design, Setting, and Participants This longitudinal cohort study used data from Project Viva, a prebirth cohort that enrolled pregnant women in eastern Massachusetts from April 22, 1999, to July 31, 2002. Participants included 570 children with available peripheral blood DNA methylation data, complete neighborhood characteristics, and complete covariates. Data were analyzed from August 19, 2024, to August 21, 2026. Exposures Neighborhood exposome profiles at birth derived from 22 census tract–level characteristics across 4 domains (area deprivation, social fragmentation, population density, and environmental quality) using self-organizing maps. Main Outcomes and Measures EAA was calculated at 3, 8, and 13 years of age using the Horvath, Skin &amp;amp; Blood, and Wu epigenetic clocks. Trajectories were identified using latent class linear mixed models. Associations between neighborhood profiles and EAA trajectories were estimated using multinomial mixed models. Results Among 570 children (mean [SD] age at early childhood, 3.2 [0.4] years; 305 [53.5%] male), 3 EAA trajectory groups (stable, increasing, and decreasing for the Horvath and Skin &amp;amp; Blood clocks or low-baseline for the Wu clock) and 3 neighborhood profiles were identified. Compared with profile 1 (suburban, lowest adverse exposures [n = 278]), children born into profile 2 (urban, high residential instability and single-person households, and highway proximity [n = 168]) had greater odds of increasing EAA for the Wu clock (adjusted odds ratio, 1.67 [95% CI, 1.03-2.69]). Profile 3 (urban, high socioeconomic deprivation and pollution [n = 124]) showed no associations. Conclusions and Relevance In this longitudinal cohort study, birth into neighborhoods characterized by high residential instability and single-person households and highway proximity was associated with increasing Wu EAA trajectories across childhood. These findings suggest that early-life neighborhood conditions, encompassing both social and physical environmental factors, may represent targets for interventions aimed at reducing long-term disease risk. Further research is needed to clarify the implications of these findings for later health and prevention.
