item.description:
Authors: Ashley S. Felix, Caitlin E. Meade, Jeffrey J. Wing, Simran A. Kanal, Laura M. Chambers, Britton Trabert, Jennifer A. Sinnott
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2644045
Abstract: Importance Racial and ethnic disparities exist in clinical trial enrollment, but whether such disparities exist in geographic availability of uterine cancer trials is unknown. Objective To examine associations between race and ethnicity and county-level presence and rates of available uterine cancer clinical trials. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study linked Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Research Plus; Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov; and American Community Survey data of adult patients (aged ≥18 years) diagnosed with uterine cancer between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2021. The data analysis was performed between November 10, 2025, and September 9, 2026. Exposures Race and ethnicity categorized as American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black, Hispanic (any race), Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and White. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes were county-level presence and rate of interventional uterine cancer trials. Hurdle models were used to estimate racial and ethnic differences in the odds of residing in a county with at least 1 trial and among patients in counties with trial availability, differences in rates of trials per person. Models accounted for county clustering and were adjusted for patient characteristics. Results Among 155 811 patients in the cohort (median [IQR] age at diagnosis, 62 [55-69] years; 1055 identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native [0.7%], 12 753 as Asian [8.2%], 16 303 as Black [10.5%], 23 177 as Hispanic [14.9%], 2175 as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander [1.4%], and 100 348 as White [64.4%] race and ethnicity), 121 525 (78.0%) resided in a county with at least 1 available trial. Trial availability was observed among 58.0% of American Indian or Alaska Native patients, 94.3% of Asian patients, 77.7% of Black patients, 86.1% of Hispanic patients, 90.3% of Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander patients, and 74.1% of White patients. Compared with White patients, higher odds of residing in counties with at least 1 available trial were found for Asian (odds ratio [OR], 5.83; 95% CI, 4.83-7.12), Black (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.07-1.30), Hispanic (OR, 2.18; 95% CI, 1.80-2.63), and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (OR, 3.34; 95% CI, 2.17-5.66) patients, whereas American Indian or Alaska Native patients had lower odds (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.39-0.61). Among patients in counties with at least 1 trial, fewer available trials per person were found for Asian (rate ratio [RR], 0.69; 95% CI, 0.65-0.74), Hispanic (RR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.52-0.61), and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.80-0.95) patients compared with White patients. Conclusions and Relevance This cohort study of patients with uterine cancer found that racial and ethnic patterns in geographic trial availability differed by how availability was measured. The presence of any trial may not fully capture geographic access to clinical trial opportunities.

item.description:
Authors: Stephanie A. S. Staras, Carma L. Bylund, Matthew J. Gurka, Lindsay A. Thompson, Marta D. Hansen, Tuo Lin, Pengchen Wang, Gabriela Sanchez, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642247
Abstract: Importance Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination rates among adolescents remain below recommendations. Objective To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician communication training and parent-targeted text messages at increasing HPV vaccination among children aged 11 to 12 years. Design, Setting, and Participants This doubly randomized, 2-level nested clinical trial was conducted from February 2022 to September 2024 among clinicians at 30 pediatric primary care clinics in Florida, children aged 10 to 12 years who had not received any of the 3 adolescent HPV vaccines, and their parents. Interventions occurred for 1 year, and vaccine records were collected for 2 years. Interventions Clinics were randomized 1:1:1 to 3 training groups: (1) the bundled approach, which presents the HPV vaccine in the middle of 2 other recommended vaccines; (2) the focused approach, which emphasizes cancer prevention; and (3) deferred, which offered clinicians the opportunity to participate in the focused training after the trial concluded. Clinicians in the first 2 groups completed a 1-hour communication training and a 5-minute booster session. Patients within clinics were randomized 1:1:1 to 3 text message groups, aligned with the communication strategies: (1) bundled, (2) focused, and (3) no text messages. Parents were sent text messages at the start of the study or prior to their child’s 11th birthday as well as prior to appointments. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were HPV vaccine initiation (receipt of first dose) and completion (receipt of second dose). Analyses accounted for clinic-level clustering. Effects were analyzed as randomized and text messages as received. Results At baseline, 59 clinicians (44 [75%] female; 12 [20%] Asian, 21 [36%] Hispanic, and 21 [36%] non-Hispanic White) within 30 randomized clinics were included, with 17 randomized to the focused group, 21 to the bundled group, and 21 to the deferred group. A total of 7234 children were aged 10 (3576 [49%]), 11 (2617 [36%]), and 12 (1041 [14%]) years at study start (1673 [23%] Hispanic, 1001 [14%] non-Hispanic Black, and 1210 [17%] non-Hispanic White). A total of 28 clinics (93%), 50 clinicians (85%), and 6498 children (90%) completed the 2-year follow-up. The mean pre-post clinic-level difference for HPV vaccine initiation was 28.2 (95% CI, 25.3-31.1) percentage points and for completion was 16.1 (95% CI, 13.3-18.9) percentage points. Risk ratios for clinician training and text messaging did not differ between groups for initiation or completion. Among patients whose parents received text messages vs not, the risk ratio for initiation was 1.17 (95% CI, 1.08-1.26) and for completion was 1.29 (95% CI, 1.06-1.56). Conclusions and Relevance In this study of Florida children aged 10 to 12 years, clinic-level HPV vaccination increased over time. No differences in HPV vaccination by random assignment of clinician training or text messages were detected. When received, text messages were associated with higher HPV vaccination. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05006833

item.dc:creator: Abigail Wilpers
Bonnie Zapolin
Katie Francis
Amy B. Powne

item.description:
Authors: Abigail Wilpers, Bonnie Zapolin, Katie Francis, Amy B. Powne, Isha Suba, Dana Zapolin, John Abdelshaheed, Jasmine Mohanlall, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642991
Abstract: Importance Maternal-fetal surgery has expanded rapidly in the US, but how insurance coverage supports delivery of this specialized, high-cost care has not been systematically characterized. Objective To characterize publicly ascertainable information about how Medicaid programs and large commercial insurers cover procedures used in maternal-fetal surgery. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional descriptive study analyzed insurance coverage policies in the US from March through August 2025. Medicaid programs and large commercial insurers were selected based on national market share. Exposure Insurance coverage policies for maternal-fetal surgery–related procedures were assessed using publicly available fee schedules and structured outreach to payer representatives. Main Outcomes and Measures Coverage status (covered, not covered, or data not available) for 19 maternal-fetal surgery–related Current Procedural Terminology ( CPT ) and Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) codes and 5 comparator codes. Results The study included 50 state Medicaid programs and 30 large commercial insurers. Among Medicaid programs, coverage was high for nonspecific or individual components of procedures (eg, intrauterine transfusion: 49 of 49 available determinations [100%]) but incomplete and highly variable for codes specific to comprehensive interventions (eg, 6 of 36 available determinations [16.7%] for in utero sacrococcygeal teratoma resection). Among 44 states with available determinations for both code types, mean (SD) coverage was higher for CPT codes than S-codes (86.3% [14.1%] vs 53.0% [37.0%]; P &amp;lt; .001), with consistent findings in sensitivity analyses. The median (range) proportion of MFS-related codes covered per state was 14.5 (0-19) of 19 codes (76.3%). Among 5 commercial insurers with data, all 5 (100.0%) reported coverage of all 4 S-codes representing comprehensive interventions. Conclusions and Relevance In this study, coverage of maternal-fetal surgery–related codes was incomplete and variable, and transparency in commercial coverage policies was limited. These findings suggest that coverage uncertainty may complicate health-system planning and financing for this increasingly used, high-cost care.

item.title: Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities in Preschoolers With Bilateral Cerebral Palsy

Geoffroy Saussez
Josselin Demas

item.description:
Authors: Rodrigo Araneda, Daniela Ebner-Karestinos, Julie Paradis, Geoffroy Saussez, Josselin Demas, Rodolphe Bailly, Sandra Bouvier, Astrid Carton de Tournai, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643492
Abstract: Importance Intensive interventions for children with cerebral palsy (CP) have traditionally focused on the upper extremities, despite frequent impairments in gross motor function and the critical period of motor development occurring before age 5 years. Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities (HABIT-ILE) has demonstrated efficacy in improving manual dexterity and gross motor function in school-aged children, but evidence in preschool children with bilateral CP remains limited. Objective To determine whether early HABIT-ILE improves gross motor function more than usual unstructured motor activities in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter randomized clinical trial was conducted between December 2019 and December 2021. Recruitment was from European university hospitals, CP-specialized centers, and spontaneous applications at 4 sites: Brussels, Belgium; Brest and Angers, France; and Pisa, Italy. Children aged 12 to 59 months with spastic or dyskinetic bilateral CP who were able to follow instructions were included. Exclusion criteria were uncontrolled seizures, scheduled botulinum toxin injections or orthopedic surgery during the 6 months before or during the study period, severe visual or cognitive impairments, and contraindications to magnetic resonance imaging. Data were analyzed in May 2024. Interventions Children were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive 2 weeks of usual motor activity, including usual rehabilitation (control group), or 2 weeks (50 hours) of HABIT-ILE (HABIT-ILE group). Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was Gross Motor Function Measure-66 (GMFM-66; range, 0-100, with lower scores indicating lesser gross motor ability). Secondary outcomes included Both Hand Assessment (BoHA), Melbourne Assessment 2, Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory-Computer Adaptive Test (PEDI-CAT), and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM). Assessments were performed at baseline (immediately before intervention) and 2 weeks and 3 months after baseline. Results Among 49 preschool children with CP (mean [SD] age, 40.18 [11.53] months; 18 girls [36.7%] and 31 boys [63.3%]), Gross Motor Function Classification levels were I in 5 children, II in 14 children, III in 17 children, and IV or V in 13 children and Mini-Manual Ability Classification levels were I in 10 children, II in 27 children, III in 7 children, and IV or V in 6 children. Change in mean (SD) GMFM-66 score from baseline to 3 months was significantly greater in the HABIT-ILE group (5.01 [2.52] logits) than the control group (0.70 [1.98] logits) (adjusted mean difference [aMD] in score, 4.33 logits; 95% CI, 3.03-5.62 logits; P &amp;lt; .001). Likewise, mean (SD) scores favored the HABIT-ILE group vs the control group for secondary outcomes of BoHA (5.32 [4.47] vs 0.13 [5.16]; aMD, 5.15; 95% CI, 2.23-8.08; P &amp;lt; .001), PEDI-CAT mobility domain (1.70 [2.18] vs −0.40 [4.38]; aMD, 2.27; 95% CI, 0.20-4.33; P = .03), and COPM performance (4.22 [1.61] vs 1.14 [1.35]; aMD, 3.55; 95% CI, 2.86-4.24; P &amp;lt; .001) and satisfaction (4.37 [1.38] vs 1.15 [1.63]; aMD, 3.11; 95% CI, 2.25-3.97; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, early HABIT-ILE significantly improved upper and lower extremities motor performance in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP at 3 months after the intervention. These findings suggest that HABIT-ILE is effective in improving gross motor function in preschool-aged children with bilateral CP. Trial Registration Clinicaltrial.gov Identifier: NCT04020354

item.description:
Authors: Laurie A. Lee, Jennifer R. Foster, Karla D. Krewulak, Dana Rhyno, Molly J. Ryan, Corey Slumkoski, Martha Walls, Neda Zafranchi-Moghadam, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643825
Abstract: Importance Family presence supports critically ill children, yet pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) policies remain inconsistent, creating inequities in access to parents or caregivers. Clear guidance is needed to support equitable, child-centered policy development. Objective To generate evidence-informed and knowledge user–informed recommendations for family presence policies in PICUs. Design, Setting, and Participants This survey study, conducted through surveys and virtual meetings, used a modified Delphi consensus process. Candidate items were derived from family presence guidance documents and PICU family presence research (environmental scan; scoping review; surveys and interviews with patients, families, and health care professionals; and focus groups). Items were organized into themes covering policy priorities; policy-making responsibilities; baseline and emergency policies; and policy communication, enforcement, and revision. From February 2024 to February 2025, panelists completed 2 rating rounds and 1 virtual meeting, with follow-up meetings and member-checking to incorporate input across knowledge user groups. Knowledge users included former PICU patients, family members, clinicians, and policymakers (hospital and PICU administrators and infection prevention and control specialists) from across Canada. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcome was consensus-derived policy priorities and recommendations for PICU family presence during baseline operations and emergency situations. Results Forty-three knowledge users, including 5 patients, 12 family members, 21 clinicians, and 5 policymakers (35 self-reported women or girls [81.4%]), agreed on 10 policy priorities and 44 recommendations. Key messages included that children should be at the center of policy-related decision-making and always have access to at least 2 primary caregivers; families should determine sibling presence and assume responsibility for it; policies should recognize the importance of visitors beyond family for the child’s well-being; and policies should be flexible, adapting to different situations while adhering to core priorities. Recommendations addressed who should make policies; communication, enforcement, and change processes; number, type (eg, parents or caregivers, siblings, and visitors), and timing of bedside presence; family movement and supports; and approaches to personal protective equipment and infectious symptoms to preserve family presence, including during emergencies. Conclusions and Relevance This survey study with consensus-based recommendations for PICU family presence provided a framework for policy design in routine and emergency contexts. The recommendations emphasized the patient’s best interest and continued access to at least 2 primary caregivers. They supported context-specific and unit-specific policy design and may be broadly applicable across children’s hospitals.

item.title: Procalcitonin- and Presepsin-Guided Antibiotics for Early-Onset Sepsis in Preterm Infants
item.dc:creator: Carlo Dani

item.description:
Authors: Carlo Dani, Chiara Poggi, Carlo Pietrasanta, Camilla Cattaneo, Monica Fumagalli, Massimo Agosti, Simona Perniciaro, Marcello Napolitano, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643418
Abstract: Importance Early administration of antibiotics in the absence of proven sepsis, such as for treatment of early-onset sepsis (EOS), has been associated with adverse outcomes in very preterm infants. Reference values for procalcitonin (PCT) and presepsin (P-SEP) have been established in preterm infants. Objective To determine whether PCT- and P-SEP–guided antibiotic treatment for EOS was noninferior to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity. Design, Setting, and Participants This randomized multicenter noninferiority clinical trial was conducted in 17 Italian neonatal intensive care units between June 1, 2023, and January 31, 2025, among preterm infants born at 25 weeks and 0 days to 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation. Interventions Enrolled infants were randomly allocated to receive either PCT- and P-SEP–guided antibiotic treatment, administered if PCT and P-SEP levels exceeded prespecified thresholds, or universal antibiotic treatment for EOS. Main Outcomes and Measures The composite primary outcome was defined as survival without late-onset sepsis (LOS), bronchopulmonary dysplasia, grade 3 or 4 intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), grade 2 or higher necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), or stage 3 or higher retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). The prespecified noninferiority margin was −5 percentage points. Both a primary intention-to-treat analysis and a secondary per-protocol analysis were performed, as recommended for noninferiority trials. Results The study enrolled and randomized 283 very preterm infants (mean [SD] gestational age, 30.2 [2.2] weeks; 161 girls [57%]); 143 received procalcitonin- and presepsin-guided treatment and 140 received universal antibiotic treatment. The primary outcome did not differ between the PCT- and P-SEP–guided treatment group and the universal antibiotic treatment groups (76 of 143 [53%] vs 77 of 140 [55%]; risk difference, −1.8 percentage points; 90% CI, −11.9 to 8.3 percentage points; P = .32). Noninferiority of PCT- and P-SEP–guided treatment compared with universal treatment was not demonstrated, because the lower bound of the 2-sided 90% CI crossed the prespecified noninferiority margin. The risk differences for LOS, IVH, NEC, PVL, ROP, and death were not significantly different between the groups. PCT and P-SEP values were not different between the groups. No patient developed EOS. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial conducted among neonates born between 25 weeks and 0 days and 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation, a PCT- and P-SEP–guided strategy for the treatment of EOS did not demonstrate noninferiority to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity. Within the limits of this study, these findings do not support the routine use of a biomarker-guided approach as an alternative to universal treatment for this high-risk population. Trial Registration Clinicaltrials.gov identifier: NCT05796115

item.title: Eating Disorders in Individuals With Celiac Disease and Their Biological First-Degree Relatives
item.dc:creator: Jialu Yao
Jiangwei Sun
David Bergman
Karl Mårild
Shengxin Liu
Peter H. R. Green
Mariel Arvizu
Cynthia M. Bulik
item.description:
Authors: Jialu Yao, Jiangwei Sun, David Bergman, Karl Mårild, Shengxin Liu, Peter H. R. Green, Mariel Arvizu, Cynthia M. Bulik, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643815
Abstract: Importance Patients with celiac disease (CD) may face elevated risk of eating disorders, potentially due to genetic susceptibility and psychosocial factors of a gluten-free diet. However, up-to-date population-based evidence is scarce, and whether any excess risk extends to biological first-degree relatives (bFDRs) remains unclear. Objective To investigate the risk of eating disorders in patients with CD and their bFDRs, including parents, full siblings, and offspring. Design, Setting, and Participants A nationwide multigenerational cohort study of patients with celiac disease in Sweden, observed from January 2002 to December 2023. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to August 2026. From Sweden’s 28 histopathology departments, patients with biopsy-confirmed CD diagnosed 2002 to 2023 were identified. Each patient was matched with fewer than or equal to 5 general population reference individuals; bFDRs of patients with CD and reference individuals were also identified. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was any eating disorder. The adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) for eating disorders diagnosed at age 6 years or older were estimated using Cox regression and flexible parametric survival models for the overall and time-varying estimates, respectively. Results This study included 37 853 patients with CD (23 704 [62.6%] female; median [IQR] age at index date 28.7 [11.7-53.0] years ) and 185 159 reference individuals. Over 10.9 years median follow-up (IQR, 5.9-15.8 years), 485 patients with CD and 1578 reference individuals were diagnosed with any eating disorder. CD was associated with an increased hazard for eating disorders (aHR, 1.39; 95% CI,1.27-1.53), most apparent during the first 5 years of follow-up. Over 20 years of follow-up, 1 extra eating disorder case was expected per 222 patients with CD. In contrast, there was no hazard elevation for any eating disorder among CD-bFDRs (53 435 parents: aHR, 0.82 [0.61-1.12]; 48 743 siblings: aHR, 1.11 [0.99–1.24]; 38 695 offspring: aHR, 1.05 [0.92-1.20]). Sensitivity analyses mitigating information bias and residual confounding largely aligned with main findings. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of patients with CD, a moderately increased eating disorders risk particularly during the first 5 years of follow-up was observed, although the absolute risk was low. This increased risk did not extend to bFDRs of patients with CD. Clinical vigilance toward disordered eating is important among patients with newly diagnosed CD.

item.title: Cumulative Stress and Health Care Utilization Among US Service Members
item.dc:creator: Daniel F. López-Cevallos
Claire A. Kolaja
Edward Chauca
Scott C. Roesch
Neika Sharifian
Felicia R. Carey
Matthew A. Allison
Sheila F. Castañeda
item.description:
Authors: Daniel F. López-Cevallos, Claire A. Kolaja, Edward Chauca, Scott C. Roesch, Neika Sharifian, Felicia R. Carey, Matthew A. Allison, Sheila F. Castañeda, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643810
Abstract: Importance Military personnel experience unique occupational stressors, which, combined with other life stressors, may substantially impact their health readiness. Stress exposure is known to be associated with health and health care concerns in civilian populations, but little is known as to whether these associations are present among US service members. Objective To evaluate the association between individual stressors, cumulative stress exposure, and health care utilization (HCU) among a contemporary sample of US service members. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective cohort analysis used self-reported survey data from the Millennium Cohort Study and up to 3 years of inpatient and outpatient HCU data from Military Health System electronic health records (2020-2023) from US active-duty service members who first completed a Millennium Cohort Study baseline survey in 2020 and 2021. Data were analyzed from January to May 2026. Exposure Self-reported stress exposure (adverse childhood experiences, stressful life events, discrimination, bullying, hazing, and combat experiences) was assessed in 2020 and 2021. Main Outcomes and Measures Inpatient, outpatient, and total HCU patient-days were calculated. Negative binomial regression models examined the HCU association with cumulative and individual stress exposures, adjusting for demographic and military characteristics. Results A total of 34 731 service members were included in the analytic sample (33 252 [95.8%] were young adults aged 17-34 years; 9906 [28.5%] were female). They spent a mean (SD) of 17.74 (19.10) days (median [IQR], 12 [2-23] days) in outpatient and 0.61 (4.98) days (median [IQR], 0 [0-0] days) in inpatient care across a mean (SD) follow-up period of 2.08 (0.84) years. Higher cumulative stress exposure was associated with greater total (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 1.54; 95% CI, 1.50-1.57), inpatient (IRR, 2.28; 95% CI, 2.21-2.35), and outpatient (IRR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.47-1.54) HCU. Individual stressors, particularly adverse childhood experiences and stressful life events, were also associated with greater HCU. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of contemporary US active-duty service members, increased stress exposure was positively associated with greater HCU. Identifying and triaging various stress exposures during outpatient visits can support better access to inpatient care for service members. In turn, these efforts may translate into better patient outcomes, medical readiness, and military health system improvements.

item.title: Civil Society Organization–Led Home Visit Intervention to Reduce Unintentional Child Injury in Rural China
item.dc:creator: Pan Wen
Ziyue Tan
Jing Zhuang
Xiaodong Chen
Xiujuan Li
Yaogui Lu
Liping Li
item.description:
Authors: Pan Wen, Ziyue Tan, Jing Zhuang, Xiaodong Chen, Xiujuan Li, Yaogui Lu, Liping Li
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643140
Abstract: Importance Unintentional injuries are a leading cause of childhood death and disability, but evidence on scalable home visit interventions in rural settings is limited. Objective To evaluate whether a civil society organization–led home visit intervention can reduce unintentional injuries among children and improve caregiver and household safety. Design, Setting, and Participants This outcome assessor–blinded cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 24 rural communities in Guizhou and Shaanxi, China, from May 6 to October 1, 2025. After baseline assessment, communities were randomized as clusters in a 1:1 ratio. Participants were households with children aged 3 to 12 years. Interventions Control communities received routine social worker home visits; intervention communities received routine services plus 3 monthly structured visits with home safety and first aid tool kits and a follow-up visit at month 4. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was caregiver-reported cumulative child unintentional injury incidence during 4 months, a subjective outcome with caregivers unblinded to group allocation. Secondary outcomes were caregiver knowledge, safety attitudes, and supervisory behaviors, with scores ranging from 0 to 40, 0 to 8, and 0 to 80, respectively, with higher scores indicating better knowledge, more positive safety attitudes, and more appropriate supervisory behaviors, respectively, and household environmental hazards, with scores ranging from 0 to 230 and higher scores indicating more household environmental hazards and a less safe home environment. Generalized estimating equations accounted for clustering. Results Among 24 randomized clusters, caregivers (mean [SD] age, 45.4 [13.0] years; 271 [75.3%] female) and children (mean [SD] age, 8.6 [2.3] years, 198 [55.0%] female) from 360 households were enrolled, with 180 each randomized to intervention and control groups. After baseline, 9 households withdrew with missing outcome data; all 360 households were included in the intention-to-treat analyses with multiple imputation. Injury occurred in 21 of 178 households (11.8%) with observed outcomes in the intervention group and 33 of 173 (19.1%) in the control group. The intervention was associated with lower injury odds (adjusted odds ratio, 0.36 [95% CI, 0.18-0.73]; P = .005). At month 4, adjusted mean differences favored the intervention for supervisory behaviors (17.08 [95% CI, 14.71-19.46] points) and household environmental hazards (−36.66 [95% CI, −42.87 to −30.46] points). Conclusions and Relevance In this cluster randomized clinical trial of households with children aged 3 to 12 years, a civil society organization–led home visit intervention reduced caregiver-reported unintentional injuries and improved caregiver supervisory behaviors and household safety during the 4-month intervention period. Longer follow-up is needed to assess durability of the response. Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2500098928

item.dc:creator: Alison Reid
Amina Tran
Suparna Thakali
Daniel Wetterskog

Anna Wingate
Priyanka Patel

item.description:
Authors: Alison Reid, Amina Tran, Suparna Thakali, Daniel Wetterskog, Francesco Orlando, Anna Wingate, Priyanka Patel, Aidan Cole, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643400
Abstract: Importance Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is increasingly used for oligoprogressive prostate cancer, but the duration of disease control is highly variable. Objective To evaluate time to progression based on circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) prior to SBRT. Design, Setting, and Participants Between October 17, 2018, and February 1, 2023, the phase 2 prospective, single-arm, nonrandomized clinical TRAP (Targeted Radiotherapy in Androgen-Suppressed Prostate Cancer Patients) trial evaluated SBRT to treat 81 patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and 2 or fewer metastases and imaging evidence of progression while receiving an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI). Plasma DNA was collected at 1 or 2 points prior to SBRT and centrally tested for ctDNA using the next-generation sequencing assay PCF_SELECT. Data were collected prospectively using electronic trial case report forms. Data were extracted November 26, 2025. The median follow-up was 24.5 (IQR, 23.7-36.3) months. Exposures Progressing metastases were treated with SBRT, and patients were followed up with clinical assessments, serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) tests, and imaging. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome measure was time to progression, defined as an increase in serum prostate-specific antigen level of 25% or greater from the post-SBRT nadir, radiologic or symptomatic progression, clinician decision to stop ARPI, or death from any cause. The secondary outcomes were time to next therapy or death from any cause. All end points were measured from time of final SBRT treatment. Results Of 77 patients with evaluable blood samples taken prior to SBRT, 19 (24.7%) were in the ctDNA-positive group. The 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate was 21.1% (95% CI, 6.6%-41.0%) for the ctDNA-positive group compared with 58.3% (95% CI, 44.5%-69.8%) for the ctDNA-negative group. The median PFS was 3.0 (95% CI, 2.7-5.9) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 7.8 (95% CI, 5.9-11.4) months for the ctDNA negative group (log rank test, P = .003 at 5% significance level). The median time to initiation of a new therapy or death was 15.3 (95% CI, 4.7-26.0) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 29.6 (95% CI, 17.8-37.6) months for the ctDNA-negative group. The median overall survival was 27.2 (95% CI, 19.2 to undefined) months for the ctDNA-positive group and 33.6 (95% CI, 28.4-38.2) months for the ctDNA-negative group. Conclusions and Relevance These findings suggest that for patients with oligoprogression and no ctDNA, SBRT and continued ARPI could be considered a valid option for prolonging disease control. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03644303
